analysis.one_liner: Sets a national goal to cut child poverty in half and requires annual government reporting to track it.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2023 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law a national policy goal of cutting the number of children living in poverty by half within five years. It would require the Department of Health and Human Services and the Census Bureau to publish an annual child poverty rate using an inflation-adjusted supplemental poverty measure, including data for Puerto Rico and other territories and corrections for underreported income. It would also commission the National Academy of Sciences to report every year on which federal policies actually reduce child poverty, and to update its 2019 roadmap on how to cut child poverty. The bill spends no money on benefits directly; it is an accountability and measurement bill, authorizing only a few million dollars for the reporting work.
analysis.who_benefits: Children living in or near poverty are the intended beneficiaries, but only indirectly: the bill would give Congress and the public a single, consistent annual number for child poverty, broken out by depth of poverty and racial and ethnic groups, and independent annual analysis of which federal programs are working. That makes it harder for policymakers to claim poverty progress that the data does not support, and easier for advocates to point to an official national goal when programs like the expanded Child Tax Credit come up for renewal. The Census Bureau, HHS, and the National Academies receive small authorizations (under about $9 million total over the years covered) to do the work.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares it the policy of the United States to cut child poverty in half within five years and directs special attention to children in deep poverty and to racial and ethnic groups with the highest poverty rates [S3].

It requires an annual, inflation-adjusted supplemental child poverty measure, released in a single file alongside the Census Bureau's annual income, poverty, and health insurance report, so there is one official yearly number for child poverty [S2] [S3].

It commissions annual National Academy of Sciences reports analyzing how federal policies and programs affect child poverty, with projections of future effects, and an updated roadmap of evidence-based ways to reduce child poverty and intergenerational poverty [S2] [S3].
It would extend official poverty measurement to Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa, where no comparable measure currently exists [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Essentially no one pays directly. The bill authorizes small appropriations for the measurement and reporting work — roughly $2 million for the territories and income-data corrections, $1 million to $1.2 million per year through 2033 for the annual reports, and $2.2 million each for the updated roadmap and the intergenerational poverty report — drawn from general federal revenue. No industry, taxpayer group, or program bears a material cost. Any cost to policymakers is political: the bill creates an official five-year goal against which their record can be measured.

drawbacks.text: The bill reduces no one's poverty by itself. It sets a goal and builds reporting, but contains no benefit expansion, tax credit change, or program funding; if policymakers ignored the reports, child poverty would not move [S2] [S3].
The five-year goal is stated as a matter of national policy without any enforcement mechanism, penalty, or required action if the target is missed, so critics could fairly call it symbolic [S3].

The reporting system carries real but modest costs — several million dollars in authorizations over roughly a decade — and adding an anchored measure alongside the Census Bureau's existing official and supplemental poverty measures creates a third poverty statistic that could confuse public debate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is genuinely small: a few million dollars for statistics and independent analysis, with no benefit cuts or industry losses attached. The honest limitation is on the benefit side — this is infrastructure for accountability, not relief. Its value depends entirely on whether Congress and future administrations respond to what the new annual numbers and National Academies reports show. As a transparency measure it is well designed and inexpensive; as an anti-poverty measure it does nothing on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2023, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey introduced the bill on September 21, 2023, joined by Senators Tammy Baldwin and Sherrod Brown [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was its only action of record [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gains materially from the bill's death, because it would have cost almost nothing and imposed no obligations on any industry. The status quo continues: there is no statutory national child poverty reduction goal, and child poverty data continues to be published under the Census Bureau's existing measures without the annual independent analysis this bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no goal was created

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Child Poverty Reduction Act of 2023 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Tammy Baldwin and Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senators from Wisconsin and Ohio; original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only two cosponsors it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral in September 2023 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and the bill drew only two cosponsors, both Democrats; no Republican signed on and the record shows no Republican support [S4].

industries.industry: National Academy of Sciences (and government statistical agencies)
industries.note: The bill would have directed about $9 million in authorizations over a decade to the National Academies, HHS, and the Census Bureau for child poverty measurement and analysis. This is a small professional-services gain for research institutions, with the work producing information the public would use at no charge.
